name: GlyNAC
lead: GlyNAC is a combination of two amino acids, glycine and N-acetylcysteine (NAC, a precursor of cysteine), that are the building blocks limiting the body's synthesis of the antioxidant tripeptide glutathione. It is sold over the counter as a dietary supplement and has been studied mainly as an intervention for age-related glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.[4][14]

The concept was developed by Rajagopal Sekhar and colleagues at Baylor College of Medicine, whose group has published most of the human work on it, beginning with an open-label trial in older people with HIV in 2020 and a pilot trial in older adults in 2021.[4][8][15] A randomized trial in older adults followed in 2023.[7] The researchers report improvements in glutathione levels, inflammation markers, insulin resistance, muscle strength, cognition and body composition.[4][7]

The published human trials are small, were largely run by one research group, and enrolled older adults rather than people seeking cosmetic changes. No study has examined effects on facial appearance or skin; the appearance-relevant outcomes that have been measured are muscle strength and body composition, and reviews describe the evidence as promising but preliminary.[6][4][2]

GlyNAC is discussed mostly in longevity and biohacking circles rather than classic looksmaxxing forums; its link to appearance runs through muscle, body composition and physical function in ageing, and through the broader role glutathione plays in cellular antioxidant defence.[4][27]

paras: GlyNAC is used as a longevity-oriented supplement. The rationale is that glutathione levels fall with age, partly because the amino acids glycine and cysteine become less available, and that supplying both together might restore glutathione and reduce oxidative stress.[4]

The appearance angle runs through body composition and physical function rather than a cosmetic claim: the Baylor group reports that GlyNAC supplementation in older adults was associated with better muscle strength, physical function and body composition, outcomes that bear on how muscular and capable a person looks and moves as they age.[4][7] No trial has tested skin, hair or facial outcomes.

N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a prodrug of the amino acid L-cysteine and raises glutathione levels in the body. As a medicine it is the antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and a mucolytic that loosens thick mucus; it was patented in 1960 and entered medical use in the late 1960s and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[23] Oral NAC commonly causes nausea and vomiting, and oral bioavailability is low, around 6 to 10 percent.[23] Amazon removed NAC products from its store in 2021 after FDA concerns about whether NAC qualified as a supplement, and relisted them in August 2022.[23]

Glycine is the simplest amino acid, is a major structural component of collagen and also acts as a neurotransmitter.[1] In the GlyNAC rationale it supplies the glycine needed for the final step of glutathione synthesis, in which glycine is added to gamma-glutamylcysteine.[3]

Glutathione is a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine and glycine. The glutamate-cysteine bond is a gamma linkage, which protects it from breakdown by common peptidases. It is made in two ATP-dependent steps, with glutamate-cysteine ligase as the rate-limiting enzyme and glutathione synthetase adding glycine to finish the molecule.[27]

Wikipedia describes glutathione as an antioxidant that helps protect cells from reactive oxygen species, peroxides and heavy metals, acts as a coenzyme for glutathione peroxidases and related enzymes, helps keep vitamins C and E in their active reduced forms, and conjugates reactive metabolites such as NAPQI from paracetamol. More than 90 percent of the glutathione in healthy cells is in the reduced form.[27]

Oral glutathione itself has poor bioavailability because gut proteases break the tripeptide down and cells lack a specific carrier for it; NAC, a cysteine prodrug, is described as a way to replenish intracellular glutathione, which is the logic behind supplying its precursors instead.[27]

Glutathione is built from glutamate, cysteine and glycine. Researchers propose that in older people cysteine and glycine are the limiting supplies, and that NAC provides cysteine while glycine supplies the second amino acid.[4] Restoring glutathione is hypothesised to lower oxidative stress, improve mitochondrial fuel oxidation and reduce inflammation.[4][6]

Glycine itself is a non-essential amino acid that the body makes from serine, is a major component of collagen, and acts as a neurotransmitter.[1] NAC is an acetylated form of cysteine that is also used as a mucolytic medicine.

Sekhar's group reported that older people have glutathione deficiency and elevated oxidative stress, and tested supplementation first in aged mice, then in people.[4][14] A 2022 mouse study from the group reported lengthened lifespan with GlyNAC.[16] Human trials followed in older adults with HIV (open-label, 2020), a pilot trial in older adults (2021) and a 24-week randomized trial (2023).[15][8][7] A separate group has run a randomized trial in healthy older adults on glutathione redox status and oxidative damage.[19]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports that the idea grew from Sekhar's earlier work on glutathione deficiency and oxidative stress and that a presentation on glutathione in ageing was given in 2013; it also reports that mouse data in 2022 attracted media attention. Hacker News threads from 2022 and 2024 link to the research and show interest among technically minded readers.[3][24][25][26]

Grokipedia reports that the typical clinical preparation is a 1:1 mass ratio of glycine to NAC and that early work from Baylor's group on cysteine and glycine shortages preceded the first human publications; it should be read as AI-generated background rather than primary documentation.[3]

Trial reports describe the combination as generally well tolerated over the study periods, and a review of glutathione precursor approaches in HIV describes consistent safety signals.[4][5] Gastrointestinal effects are the usual concern with NAC. Long-term safety at the doses used in trials has not been established by published studies.

Wikipedia notes that nausea and vomiting are common with oral NAC and that rash and itching can occur with any route.[23] The 2021 and 2023 GlyNAC trials were short (about 24 weeks), and the 2023 report describes some benefits partly reversing after supplementation ended, according to Grokipedia.[3]

A 2021 open-label pilot trial in older adults reported that GlyNAC supplementation corrected glutathione deficiency and was associated with improvements in markers of oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, inflammation, insulin resistance, endothelial function, muscle strength and cognition.[8] An earlier open-label trial in older people with HIV reported similar patterns.[15]

A randomized clinical trial in older adults, published in 2023, reported that GlyNAC compared with placebo improved glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, physical function and ageing hallmarks.[7] The authors have summarised their program in a 2021 review.[4] A pilot study in people with type 2 diabetes reported improved mitochondrial fuel oxidation and lower insulin resistance.[17]

A separate randomized controlled trial in healthy older adults examined glutathione redox status and oxidative damage with glycine and NAC supplementation.[19] Reviews note that the findings on NAC are context-dependent, with benefits in people with low baseline glutathione and inconsistent results in healthy populations.[6] Registered trials include studies of glutathione-based supplementation in HIV, Alzheimer disease and post-surgical pain.[20][21][22]

Several reviews place GlyNAC among supplements with plausible benefits for muscle and physical function in ageing, while noting that independent replication and long-term data are limited.[2][6] Animal studies report effects in aged mice on brain function and lifespan.[16][12]

GlyNAC is sold as an over-the-counter supplement combining the two ingredients. Interest in it among longevity enthusiasts follows the Baylor publications; Hacker News submissions titled 'Anti-Aging Effects of GlyNAC' (2024) and 'GlyNAC supplementation reverses aging hallmarks in aging humans' (2022) received little discussion.[24][26] Proponents point to the human trials and to the group's mouse lifespan study, while reviewers caution that independent replication is limited.[16][2][6]

People interested in healthy ageing describe GlyNAC as a way to support muscle strength, physical function and body composition as they get older, which proponents link to looking and moving younger.[4][7] Reviews of mitochondrial nutrition list GlyNAC alongside MitoQ, urolithin A and omega-3 fatty acids as supplements with a plausible mechanistic basis for supporting physical function in ageing.[2]

A 2026 review of glycine and NAC in functional ageing describes NAC's effects as context-dependent, with improvements in glutathione availability and fatigue resistance in people with low baseline glutathione and inconsistent results in healthy populations, and notes that glycine derivatives show mixed results for anaerobic performance.[6] Community discussion online is modest; the Baylor papers have been shared on Hacker News with little commentary.[24][25][26]

lore.intro: GlyNAC is discussed as a longevity supplement, with the Baylor trials as the main reference point.[24][26]

claims.believers: Proponents cite the Baylor group's reports that supplementation corrected glutathione deficiency and improved markers of oxidative stress, inflammation and mitochondrial function in older adults.[7][8]
claims.experts: Reviewers describe the findings as promising but note that the trials are small, largely from one research group, and short, and that independent replication is limited.[2][6]

claims.claim: GlyNAC improves strength and body composition in older people
claims.believers: The Baylor group reports better muscle strength, physical function and body composition after supplementation.[4][7]
claims.experts: A 2024 review lists GlyNAC among supplements that may support physical function in ageing via mitochondria, while a 2026 review calls the combination a proof-of-concept needing confirmation.[2][6]

claims.believers: A 2022 mouse study from the group reported lengthened lifespan with GlyNAC, which enthusiasts cite.[16]
claims.experts: The lifespan data are from mice; a 2025 review of mouse ageing standards discusses how such claims are judged against long-lived controls, and no human lifespan study exists.[14][16]

claims.claim: Benefits depend on continuing the supplement
claims.believers: Followers of the research say effects may fade if it is stopped, as the Grokipedia summary of the 2023 trial describes.[3]
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports that some benefits partly reversed after supplementation ended in the 2023 trial.[3]
